title: Choose Resources for the Next Concrete Step
subtitle: Evaluate information and tools by fit, not by novelty or collection size.
description: Start from the output or decision you need, choose the resource that best fits that next step, check authority, freshness, licensing and security where relevant, test the smallest useful use, then keep, defer or archive it.

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose a resource because it helps the next concrete step, not merely because it is new, popular or already collected.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Name the output or decision you need, compare candidate resources on direct relevance and usability, check authority, freshness, licensing, privacy and security where they matter, try the smallest useful interaction, and record whether to keep, defer or archive the resource.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What next step was this resource meant to support, did it fit that job, what constraint did I verify, and should I keep using it, defer it or archive it?

faq.question: Does newer always mean better?
faq.answer: No. Freshness matters when information changes quickly, while stable references may remain useful for much longer. Check the update date and applicability only when they matter to the task.

faq.question: How should I evaluate a tool or plugin?
faq.answer: Check whether it supports the current task, what access it requires, whether its license and data handling fit your constraints, and whether a small reversible test is possible. Do not install or connect a tool merely to clear a resource backlog.

faq.question: What if a resource looks valuable but is not useful now?
faq.answer: Defer or archive it with enough context to find it later. Keeping every potentially useful resource in the active queue creates competition with material that supports the work already in progress.

intro.html: A resource is useful only in relation to a job. Before collecting another article, report, tool, dataset, template or course, state the output or decision you are trying to move. Then evaluate the resource against that next step rather than treating novelty, price or recency as a quality score.

sections.title: 1. Name the job for the resource
sections.html: Write the next output, decision, question or blocker the resource should support. This creates a filter: material that does not address the current job can be deferred without needing a full review.

sections.title: 2. Check the constraints that matter
sections.html: Inspect relevance and usability first. Where appropriate, also check authorship or ownership, update date, license, required permissions, privacy, data handling, compatibility and security. The necessary checks depend on whether the resource is information, software, data, a service or another kind of input.

sections.title: 3. Test the smallest useful interaction
sections.html: Read the section tied to the question, inspect a representative sample, run a safe example, or compare the tool against the immediate requirement. Stop once you have enough information to decide whether deeper use is justified.

sections.title: 4. Keep, defer or archive it
sections.html: Keep the resource active when it supports the current work and passes the relevant constraints. Defer it when it is useful for a known later step. Archive or reject it when the fit is weak, the cost is unjustified, or the permissions and risks do not match the task.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace fabricated internal project outcomes, universal freshness windows, arbitrary time and price thresholds and claimed follow-through improvements with a bounded resource-selection and evaluation workflow.
